messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Delivery Driver
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Walter had been on his delivery route for nearly two decades, but the evening it changed began like any other Tuesday in November. He was making a stop behind a commercial strip when a man stepped out from behind a metal dumpster, demanded his wallet, and struck him twice across the shoulder and jaw before snatching his gloves and disappearing into the dusk. Walter had come to believe that the world no longer operated by any reliable rules; the assault shattered his long-held conviction that showing up to work and doing the job well would keep him safe. In the days that followed, he found himself certain that if he let his mind rest on what happened, the weight of it would be too much to bear, so he began pushing the memory away before it could surface. The habit of staying constantly occupied took root quickly. Walter threw himself into his work, taking double shifts and volunteering for the longest routes across the county. He refused to sit in the breakroom, preferring to loop back through residential streets and industrial parks just to keep his hands on the wheel. He mapped his route with excessive care, logging extra stops on adjacent blocks just to keep the engine running and the dashboard lights flashing. The van became both his workplace and his refuge, a place where he could keep moving long enough to outrun the stillness that usually brought the November night back to mind. When anxiety tightened his chest in the cab, he reached for the drawer where he kept bags of chips and granola bars, eating steadily not out of hunger but to occupy his mouth and quiet the static in his head. He told himself he was just managing the stress of an older man driving alone, but the eating had become a steady, unconscious ritual. At the same time, he worked hard to keep the memory at bay, repeating delivery sequences under his breath and fixing his eyes on the next turn long before the street sign appeared. He was certain that his mind would fracture if he allowed himself to dwell on the assault, so he treated the memory like a live wire, avoiding it through sheer mental labor. Alongside these routines, a quiet but persistent uncertainty about his own judgment took hold. Walter had come to believe he could no longer trust that he would make the right call. At delivery stops, he would pause at the curb, questioning whether he had locked the cab, whether he had left a tip in the wrong place, whether the customer he passed that morning had noticed his tense posture. The world felt fundamentally unpredictable to him; a sudden shout from a porch or the glare of headlights in his rearview mirror would send his pulse racing, not because he expected another attack, but because his sense of how life should unfold had been stripped away. He avoided certain alleys and loading zones now, not out of fear alone, but because the spaces felt like mirrors of that November night. The daily patterns he had adopted over months had quietly narrowed his days. His wife noticed he stopped talking about his routes, ate dinner too quickly, and sat in the living room with the television at full volume just to keep the silence from creeping in. By spring, Walter’s double shifts had worn down his knees, and the constant grazing in the van had changed his weight and his stamina. He found himself hesitating at doorsteps, second-guessing whether he had the right package for the right house, and waking before dawn with his stomach tight. What frightened him most was not the memory itself, but the conviction that letting it in would overwhelm him, so he kept his days packed with driving, eating, and mental rehearsal. His wife had gently suggested he speak to someone, noting how his shoulders stayed drawn up and how his hands refused to rest on the steering wheel without tapping the plastic rim. Walter finally agreed, mostly because the silence at home had become heavy, and because he hoped, if only for a moment, to find a way to trust his own mind again without having to outrun it.
